note: Sourced: punto has 'Andalusian and Canary Islands origins' and took the décima espinela, quatrain coplas and the laúd from the Canaries. iberianpop is the tree's record for Iberian song with décima verse; it ends in 1800 and names Seville, so it fits the Andalusian side better than the Canarian. A Canary Islands folk record does not exist.

English Wikipedia (citing Manuel, Caribbean Currents, p. 156): twoubadou 'combined music derived from the guajiro traditions of Cuba' with méringue, brought back by Haitian cane cutters. The claim is checked as far as Wikipedia goes; the book itself was not read. Says 'guajiro traditions', not guitar style specifically. Twoubadou keeps son as principal parent.

Sourced: the punto, known in Spain as 'punto de La Habana', was taken into flamenco in the second half of the 19th century as the palo called guajira (a return trip; flamenco's own principal parent is unchanged).
